chapters.n: Hebrews opens like a sermon, not a letter. In the past God spoke to Israel’s ancestors many times and in many ways through prophets — visions, dreams, laws, and symbols. Tradition attributes this book to Paul, though the text itself names no author.

f.w: sundry times and in divers manners
f.g: In many portions and in various ways.

chapters.n: But now, in these last days, God has spoken through His Son, whom He appointed heir of everything and through whom He created the worlds.

f.w: by whom also he made the worlds

chapters.n: The Son radiates God’s glory and is the exact representation of His being. He sustains all things by His powerful word, and after cleansing us from sin He sat down at the Father’s right hand.

f.g: Greek charaktēr — exact imprint, like a stamp on a coin.

f.w: sat down on the right hand

chapters.n: He is far greater than the angels, just as the name He inherited — “Son” — is greater than theirs. Some early Jewish Christians apparently gave angels great honor; the author shows Christ is above them.
God never said to any angel, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” or “I will be his Father.” These words from the Psalms and from God’s promise to David point to Christ.

f.w: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee
I will be to him a Father

chapters.n: When God brings His Firstborn into the world, He commands all His angels to worship Him.

f.g: Firstborn — highest in rank and birthright.

f.w: let all the angels of God worship him

chapters.n: About angels, God says He makes them winds and flames of fire — powerful servants, but servants nonetheless.
But to the Son He says, “Your throne, O God, lasts forever; your royal scepter is a scepter of justice.” The Son is addressed as God and King.
Because the Son loved righteousness and hated evil, God anointed Him with the oil of joy above His companions. “Messiah” and “Christ” both mean “Anointed One.”

f.g: Festive anointing oil — a symbol of joy and royal appointment.

chapters.n: Applying Psalm 102 to Christ, the author says the Lord laid earth’s foundation and made the heavens. Latter-day Saints recognize Jehovah of the Old Testament as the premortal Christ.

f.w: laid the foundation of the earth

chapters.n: Creation will grow old and pass away like worn clothing, but the Lord remains.
He will roll up the heavens like a cloak and change them like clothes, but He is always the same, and His years never end.
God never told any angel, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.” That place belongs to the Son alone.

f.g: A conquered enemy was symbolically placed under the victor’s feet.

chapters.n: Angels are servant spirits sent out to help those who will inherit salvation. Scripture teaches angels still minister to the faithful.
Because the Son is so great, we must pay closer attention to what we have heard, so we don’t drift away like a boat slipping past its harbor.
If the message delivered through angels — the law of Moses — was binding, and every violation was justly punished,

f.g: Jewish tradition held that angels helped deliver the law at Sinai.

chapters.n: how can we escape if we ignore such a great salvation? The Lord Himself first announced it, and those who heard Him confirmed it to us.

f.g: The eyewitnesses — suggesting the author was a second-generation believer.

chapters.n: God also testified to it with signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Ghost distributed as He chose.
God did not give the angels rule over the world to come, which is the subject here.

f.g: The coming age of Christ’s reign.

chapters.n: Someone has testified in the Psalms: “What is man that you remember him, or the son of man that you care for him?”
“You made him a little lower than the angels for a while, crowned him with glory and honor, and put him over your works.”

f.w: a little lower than the angels

chapters.n: God put everything under humanity’s feet. Yet we don’t see everything under man’s control now — the promise is not yet fulfilled in us.
But we do see Jesus, made lower than the angels for a while so He could suffer death, now crowned with glory and honor. By God’s grace He tasted death for everyone. He fulfills Psalm 8 for us.
It was fitting for God, who created and sustains all things, to make the leader of our salvation complete through suffering, as He brings many children to glory.

f.g: Fully qualified, complete — not that He was ever sinful.

chapters.n: Jesus, who makes people holy, and those being made holy share one Father. So He is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.

f.w: not ashamed to call them brethren

chapters.n: As the Psalm says, “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the congregation I will sing your praise.” Psalm 22 begins with the cry Jesus uttered on the cross.

f.w: I will declare thy name unto my brethren

chapters.n: And Isaiah: “I will put my trust in Him,” and “Here am I, and the children God has given me.” Christ stands with His people as one family.

f.w: I will put my trust in him

chapters.n: Since God’s children have flesh and blood, Jesus took on the same, so that by His death He could break the power of the devil, who held the power of death.
And set free those who all their lives were enslaved by the fear of death.
He came not to help angels, but to help Abraham’s descendants — human beings.

f.g: Took hold of, came to help.

chapters.n: So He had to become like His brothers and sisters in every way, to be a merciful and faithful High Priest who makes atonement for the people’s sins. This introduces the book’s main theme: Christ as High Priest.
Because He Himself suffered when tempted, He can help those who are tempted. He knows from experience.
So, holy brothers and sisters who share a heavenly calling, focus your thoughts on Jesus — the Apostle (One sent from God) and High Priest of the faith we confess.

f.g: One sent — Christ was sent by the Father.
Confession — the faith we openly declare.

chapters.n: He was faithful to the Father who appointed Him, just as Moses was faithful in all God’s household.
Yet Jesus deserves more glory than Moses, as the builder of a house deserves more honor than the house.
Every house has a builder, but God is the builder of everything.
Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, pointing ahead to things that would be revealed later.

f.w: a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after

chapters.n: But Christ is faithful as a Son over God’s house — and we are that house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and joyful hope to the end.
The Holy Ghost speaks through Psalm 95: “Today, if you hear His voice —” The author treats scripture as the Spirit’s living voice.

f.w: To day if ye will hear his voice

chapters.n: “— don’t harden your hearts as Israel did when they rebelled in the wilderness.”

f.g: Rebellion; the Hebrew place names Meribah (“quarreling”) and Massah (“testing”).

chapters.n: “There your ancestors tested and tried Me, though they saw My works for forty years.”
“So I was angry with that generation: their hearts are always going astray, and they have not known My ways.”
“So I swore in My anger, ‘They shall not enter My rest.’” For Israel, rest meant the promised land; latter-day revelation connects God’s rest with the fulness of His glory.
Be careful, brothers and sisters, that none of you has a wicked, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
Encourage one another every day, while it is still “today,” so none of you is hardened by sin’s deceptiveness.
We share in Christ if we hold our original confidence firmly to the end.
As the Psalm keeps saying: Today, if you hear His voice, don’t harden your hearts as in the rebellion.
Who heard and yet rebelled? All who left Egypt under Moses — with a few faithful exceptions like Joshua and Caleb.
With whom was God angry for forty years? Those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the desert.
To whom did He swear they would never enter His rest? Those who disobeyed.

f.g: Or “disobeyed” — unbelief and disobedience go together.

chapters.n: So we see they couldn’t enter because of unbelief. The warning: the same can happen to us.
Since God’s promise of entering His rest still stands, we should be careful that none of us falls short of it.

f.g: Take serious care; be reverently cautious.

chapters.n: We have heard the good news just as the Israelites did, but the message didn’t help them because they didn’t combine it with faith. Latter-day scripture likewise teaches the gospel was preached anciently.

f.w: unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them

f.g: United with faith in the hearers.

chapters.n: We who believe do enter that rest. God’s works were finished at Creation, so His rest has been available all along — yet unbelievers are shut out.

f.w: As I have sworn in my wrath
from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Scripture says about the seventh day: “God rested on the seventh day from all His works.”

f.w: God did rest the seventh day

chapters.n: And in the Psalm again: “They shall not enter My rest.”
So the rest is still open for some to enter, since those who first heard the promise failed to enter because of disobedience.
So God set another day — “Today” — speaking through David centuries later: “Today, if you hear His voice, don’t harden your hearts.”

f.g: In the Psalms, attributed to David.

chapters.n: If Joshua had given them the full rest, God wouldn’t have spoken later about another day. “Jesus” here is the Greek form of Joshua, who led Israel into Canaan.

f.g: Joshua — the same name in Greek (Iēsous).

chapters.n: So there remains a Sabbath-rest for God’s people.

f.w: a rest to the people of God

chapters.n: Whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own labors, as God did from His.
So let us make every effort to enter that rest, so no one falls by following Israel’s example of disobedience.
God’s word is alive and active, sharper than a double-edged sword. It cuts to our deepest being and judges the thoughts and intentions of our hearts.

f.w: discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart

chapters.n: Nothing in creation is hidden from God. Everything is uncovered and exposed before the eyes of the One to whom we must give account.

f.w: him with whom we have to do
f.g: Him to whom we must give an account.

chapters.n: Since we have a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens — Jesus, the Son of God — let us hold firmly to the faith we profess.

f.g: As the high priest passed through the veil into the Holy of Holies.

chapters.n: Our High Priest isn’t unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. He was tempted in every way as we are, yet He never sinned.

f.w: touched with the feeling of our infirmities

chapters.n: So let us come confidently to God’s throne of grace, to receive mercy and find help just when we need it.

f.g: God’s throne pictured as a mercy seat.

chapters.n: Every high priest is chosen from among people and appointed to represent them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins.
He can deal gently with the ignorant and those who go astray, since he too is surrounded by weakness.
Because of his own weakness, he must offer sacrifices for his own sins as well as the people’s.
No one takes this honor on himself; he must be called by God, as Aaron was. This verse is often cited for the principle that priesthood authority must come by divine call.

f.w: called of God, as was Aaron

chapters.n: Likewise Christ didn’t exalt Himself to be High Priest. God appointed Him, the same God who said, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”
As another Psalm says, “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.” This order is older and greater than Aaron’s.

During His mortal life Jesus offered prayers and pleas with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverent submission — a picture of Gethsemane.

f.g: Because of his reverence, godly submission.

chapters.n: Even though He was God’s Son, He learned obedience through what He suffered.
Having been made perfect — fully qualified — He became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey Him.
God designated Him High Priest after the order of Melchizedek.
The author has much to say about this, but it’s hard to explain because the readers have become slow to understand.

f.g: Sluggish in listening, lazy in understanding.

chapters.n: By now they ought to be teachers, yet they need someone to teach them the basics of God’s word again. They need milk, not solid food.

f.w: milk, and not of strong meat

chapters.n: Anyone living on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the teaching about righteousness.
Solid food is for the mature, who by constant practice have trained their senses to tell good from evil. Spiritual growth comes through use.

So let us move beyond the elementary teachings about Christ and press on to maturity. The JST reads “not leaving the principles,” meaning we build on them rather than abandon them. The foundations include repentance and faith.

f.g: JST: “not leaving” — the first principles remain foundational.
Lifeless acts that lead to death, or ritual acts without faith.

chapters.n: Other foundational teachings are baptisms, the laying on of hands, resurrection, and eternal judgment — a list close to the first principles and ordinances of the gospel.

f.g: “Baptisms” is plural — probably distinguishing Christian baptism from other washings.

chapters.n: And with God’s help, we will move forward.
It is impossible for those who have truly been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, and shared in the Holy Ghost —

f.g: Fully given light — real spiritual knowledge.

chapters.n: — who have tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the coming age —

f.w: powers of the world to come
f.g: Miracles and spiritual gifts that foreshadow the coming kingdom.

chapters.n: — and then fall away, to be brought back to repentance. They are crucifying God’s Son all over again and publicly shaming Him. Latter-day scripture describes such complete rebellion after full knowledge as the sin of the sons of perdition.

f.w: crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh
put him to an open shame

chapters.n: Land that soaks up frequent rain and produces a good crop for the farmer receives God’s blessing.
But land producing only thorns and thistles is worthless, close to being cursed, and ends up burned.
But even though we speak this way, dear friends, we’re confident of better things for you — things that come with salvation.
God is just; He won’t forget your work and the love you showed for Him by serving the Saints, as you still do.
We want each of you to keep showing this same diligence to the very end, so your hope is fully realized.
Don’t become lazy; imitate those who inherit God’s promises through faith and patient endurance.

f.g: Sluggish, lazy — same word as “dull” in 5:11.

chapters.n: When God made His promise to Abraham, there was no one greater to swear by, so He swore by Himself.
He said, “I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants.” The Hebrew doubling emphasizes certainty.

f.w: Surely blessing I will bless thee

chapters.n: Abraham waited patiently and received what was promised — Isaac, the son of promise.
People swear by something greater than themselves, and an oath settles every argument.
God wanted to show the heirs of the promise very clearly that His purpose cannot change, so He confirmed it with an oath.
So by two unchangeable things — God’s promise and His oath — in which He cannot lie, we who have fled to Him for refuge have strong encouragement to hold onto our hope.

f.g: Like a fugitive running to a city of refuge.

chapters.n: This hope is an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It reaches behind the veil into the inner sanctuary — God’s presence.

f.g: The Holy of Holies, behind the temple veil.

chapters.n: Jesus has gone there ahead of us as our forerunner, having become a High Priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

f.g: One who runs ahead to prepare the way for others to follow.

chapters.n: The author now explains Melchizedek: king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham coming back from defeating the kings and blessed him. The Book of Mormon adds that he was a great high priest who brought his people to repentance and peace.
Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means “king of righteousness,” and “king of Salem” means “king of peace.”

f.g: Probably early Jerusalem; related to shalom, “peace.”

chapters.n: Genesis records no parents or genealogy for him, picturing an eternal priesthood. The JST clarifies that it is the priesthood order — “after the order of the Son of God” — that is without father, mother, or beginning, and that all ordained to it are made like the Son of God.

f.w: Without father, without mother, without descent
f.g: JST: the order of the priesthood, not the man, is without father or mother or end.

f.w: made like unto the Son of God

chapters.n: Think how great he was: even Abraham, the patriarch, gave him a tenth of the spoils.

f.g: Founding father of a family or nation.

chapters.n: Under the law of Moses, Levi’s descendants who held the priesthood collected tithes from their fellow Israelites — who were also descended from Abraham.
But Melchizedek, who was not from Levi’s line, collected tithes from Abraham and blessed the man who held God’s promises.
Without question, the one who gives a blessing is greater than the one who receives it.
Levitical priests are mortal men who die, but Melchizedek is portrayed in scripture as one who lives on.

f.g: Scripture records no death for him — fitting the picture of an eternal priesthood.

chapters.n: One could even say that Levi, who collects tithes, paid tithes through Abraham.
Levi was still in his ancestor Abraham’s body, so to speak, when Melchizedek met him.
If the Levitical priesthood — the basis for the law of Moses — could bring people to perfection, why would God need another priest after Melchizedek’s order instead of Aaron’s?

f.g: Completion, the full goal of salvation.

chapters.n: When the priesthood changes, the law must change too.

f.w: a change also of the law

chapters.n: Jesus came from a different tribe, one that never served at the altar.
Clearly our Lord descended from Judah, and Moses said nothing about priests from that tribe.
It’s even clearer since another priest has arisen who is like Melchizedek.
He became priest not by a law about physical descent, but by the power of an indestructible life.

f.g: A rule based on physical lineage.

chapters.n: As the Psalm testifies: “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.”
The former regulation is set aside because it was weak and couldn’t accomplish salvation.
The law made nothing perfect, but a better hope has been introduced, through which we draw near to God.
And this was confirmed with an oath.
The Levitical priests became priests without an oath, but Jesus became a priest with God’s oath: “The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind.”

f.w: The Lord sware and will not repent

chapters.n: Because of that oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.

f.g: Guarantor — one who stands behind a promise.

chapters.n: There were many Levitical priests because death kept each from continuing in office.
But Jesus lives forever, so His priesthood is permanent.

f.g: Permanent, not passing to a successor.

chapters.n: So He can completely save those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.
This is exactly the High Priest we need: holy, innocent, pure, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.
Unlike other high priests, He doesn’t need to offer sacrifices daily, first for His own sins and then for others. He offered Himself once for all.
The law appoints weak men as high priests, but God’s oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, made perfect forever.
Here’s the main point: we have such a High Priest, seated at the right hand of God’s throne in heaven.

f.g: A reverent way of saying God.

chapters.n: He serves in the true sanctuary — the heavenly one that the Lord set up, not humans.

f.g: The tent-temple Israel carried in the wilderness.

chapters.n: Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so Christ too had to have something to offer — Himself.
If He were on earth He wouldn’t be a priest under the law, since there are already priests offering gifts by the law of Moses.
Those priests serve in a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary. God told Moses to build everything by the pattern shown him on the mountain — earthly temples reflect heavenly realities.
But Jesus has a far better ministry, because He mediates a better covenant founded on better promises.
If the first covenant had been flawless, there would have been no need for a second.
God found fault with the people and promised through Jeremiah: “The days are coming when I will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah.”
It won’t be like the covenant made with their ancestors when He led them out of Egypt, because they did not remain faithful to it.
In the new covenant God will put His laws in their minds and write them on their hearts. He will be their God and they will be His people.

f.w: they shall be to me a people

chapters.n: No one will need to tell a neighbor, “Know the Lord,” for everyone will know Him, from least to greatest.
God will be merciful toward their wrongs and remember their sins no more.
By calling the covenant “new,” God made the first one old, and what is aging is ready to disappear.

f.g: Possibly hinting the temple sacrifices would soon end.

chapters.n: The first covenant had rules for worship and an earthly sanctuary. The author now walks through the tabernacle to show how it pointed to Christ.
The tabernacle’s outer room, the Holy Place, held the lampstand and the table with the sacred bread.

f.g: Bread of the Presence — twelve loaves set before the Lord.

chapters.n: Behind the second curtain was the inner room called the Holy of Holies.

f.g: The Most Holy Place, representing God’s presence.

chapters.n: It contained the golden incense altar (or censer) and the gold-covered ark of the covenant, which held a jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant.

f.g: Probably the golden altar of incense, closely tied to the Holy of Holies.

chapters.n: Above the ark were the glorious cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat, the lid of the ark. The author says he can’t go into detail now.

f.g: Winged heavenly beings guarding God’s presence.
The ark’s gold lid, where atoning blood was sprinkled.

chapters.n: With everything arranged this way, priests regularly entered the outer room to perform their duties.
But only the high priest entered the inner room, just once a year on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood, offered for his own sins and the people’s unintentional sins.
The Holy Ghost was teaching through this arrangement that the way into God’s presence had not yet been opened while the first tabernacle still stood.

f.w: the way into the holiest of all

chapters.n: That system was a symbol for that time. Its gifts and sacrifices couldn’t cleanse the worshipper’s conscience.
These were external rules about food, drink, and ritual washings, meant to last only until God brought the new order.

f.g: Time of setting things right — the new covenant.

chapters.n: But Christ came as High Priest of the good things that have now come, serving in a greater, more perfect tabernacle, not man-made or part of this creation.
He entered the Most Holy Place once for all, not with the blood of goats and calves but with His own blood, securing eternal redemption.
If animal blood and the ashes of a red heifer could make people ceremonially clean outwardly,
how much more will Christ’s blood — who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without blemish to God — cleanse our consciences from deadening works so we can serve the living God!

f.g: Unblemished, like a perfect sacrificial lamb.

chapters.n: So Christ mediates a new covenant. His death redeems people from sins committed under the first covenant, so those called can receive the promised eternal inheritance.
The author plays on the double meaning of the Greek word for covenant, which also means “will”: a will only takes effect when the one who made it dies.

f.g: Greek diathēkē — covenant or last will.
The one who makes a will.

chapters.n: A will is valid only after death; it has no force while its maker lives.
So even the first covenant was put into effect with blood.
After Moses read all the commandments to the people, he took blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled the book and all the people.

f.w: sprinkled both the book, and all the people

f.g: A small bushy plant used to sprinkle liquids in rituals.

chapters.n: He said, “This is the blood of the covenant God commanded for you.” Jesus echoed these words at the Last Supper.

f.w: This is the blood of the testament

chapters.n: He likewise sprinkled blood on the tabernacle and all its sacred vessels.
Under the law nearly everything was cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Life is in the blood, so it symbolized a life given.

f.w: without shedding of blood is no remission

chapters.n: The earthly copies needed cleansing with these animal sacrifices, but the heavenly realities require better sacrifices.
Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary that only copied the true one, but heaven itself, to appear before God on our behalf.

f.w: to appear in the presence of God for us

chapters.n: Nor did He need to offer Himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that isn’t his own.
Otherwise He would have had to suffer many times since Creation. Instead He appeared once at the climax of the ages to remove sin by sacrificing Himself.

f.g: The culmination of the ages — the meridian of time.

chapters.n: People are destined to die once, and after that comes judgment.

f.w: appointed unto men once to die

chapters.n: So Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and He will appear a second time — not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those eagerly waiting for Him.
The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, not the reality itself. Its yearly sacrifices could never perfect those who worshipped through them.

f.w: a shadow of good things to come

f.g: The actual form, the real substance.

chapters.n: If they could, the sacrifices would have stopped, since the worshippers would have been cleansed once and no longer felt guilty.
Instead, those sacrifices served as a yearly reminder of sins.

f.w: a remembrance again made of sins

chapters.n: It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Animal sacrifices pointed to Christ but could not themselves save.
So when Christ came into the world, He said in the words of Psalm 40: “You didn’t want sacrifices and offerings, but you prepared a body for me.”

f.w: a body hast thou prepared me
Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not
f.g: God valued obedience over ritual alone.

chapters.n: “You took no pleasure in burnt offerings and sin offerings.”
“Then I said, ‘Here I am — it is written about me in the scroll — I have come to do your will, O God.’” Christ’s willing obedience is the real offering.
First the Psalm says God didn’t desire or delight in the sacrifices offered under the law —
— then He says, “I have come to do your will.” Christ sets aside the first system to establish the second.
By God’s will, we have been made holy through Jesus Christ’s offering of His body once for all.
Every priest stands day after day offering the same sacrifices repeatedly, which can never remove sins. Notice: they always stand, because their work is never finished.

f.g: There was no chair in the tabernacle — the work was never done.

chapters.n: But Christ, after offering one sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at God’s right hand — His work complete.
There He waits until His enemies are made His footstool.
By one offering He has perfected forever those who are being made holy.
The Holy Ghost also testifies to this through Jeremiah’s prophecy.
“This is the covenant I will make with them, says the Lord: I will put My laws in their hearts and write them on their minds.”

f.w: I will put my laws into their hearts

chapters.n: Then He adds, “Their sins and lawless deeds I will remember no more.”
Where sins have been forgiven, no further sacrifice for sin is needed.
So, brothers and sisters, we can confidently enter the Most Holy Place — God’s presence — through Jesus’s blood.

f.g: The Holy of Holies — God’s presence.

chapters.n: He opened a new and living way for us through the veil — His own body. When His body was torn on the cross, the temple veil tore too.

f.w: through the veil, that is to say, his flesh

chapters.n: And we have a great High Priest over God’s household.

So let us draw near to God with sincere hearts and full confidence in faith, our hearts cleansed from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water — an allusion to baptism and priestly washing.
Let us hold firmly, without wavering, to the hope we profess, for God, who promised, is faithful.
Let us think about how to stir one another up to love and good deeds.

f.g: Stir up, spur on (in a good sense).

chapters.n: Don’t give up meeting together, as some are doing, but encourage each other — all the more as you see the Day of the Lord approaching.

f.w: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together

f.g: The Day of the Lord — Christ’s coming.

chapters.n: If we deliberately keep sinning after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains — for we would be rejecting the only sacrifice there is.
Only a terrifying expectation of judgment and raging fire that will consume God’s enemies.
Anyone who rejected Moses’s law died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.
How much worse punishment is deserved by someone who tramples on God’s Son, treats as unholy the covenant blood that sanctified him, and insults the Spirit of grace?

f.w: trodden under foot the Son of God

chapters.n: We know the One who said, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,” and “The Lord will judge His people.”
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
But remember those earlier days, after you first received the light, when you endured a great struggle with suffering.

f.g: Enlightened — sometimes a term for conversion or baptism.

chapters.n: Sometimes you were publicly mocked and mistreated; at other times you stood by those who were treated that way.
You showed compassion to prisoners and joyfully accepted the seizure of your property, knowing you have a better and lasting possession.
So don’t throw away your confidence; it will be richly rewarded.
You need endurance, so that after doing God’s will you will receive what He promised.
In just a little while, the One who is coming will come and will not delay.
“My righteous one will live by faith, but if he shrinks back, I take no pleasure in him.”

f.w: the just shall live by faith

chapters.n: But we are not those who shrink back and are destroyed, but those who believe and are saved.

This famous chapter defines faith: it is the assurance of what we hope for and the conviction of realities we can’t see. The JST renders “substance” as “assurance.” Faith is confident trust that acts.

f.g: Greek hypostasis — underlying reality, title deed; JST “assurance.”

chapters.n: By faith the people of old earned God’s approval. The rest of the chapter is a “hall of faith” of these ancestors.
By faith we understand that God formed the worlds by His word, so that the visible world was not made from things that were visible.

f.w: the worlds were framed by the word of God

chapters.n: By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain, and God accepted it as righteous. Though dead, Abel still speaks to us through his example. Restoration scripture adds that Cain’s offering was made at Satan’s urging.

By faith Enoch was taken up without dying; he couldn’t be found because God had taken him. Before that, he was known as one who pleased God. Latter-day scripture describes his whole city, Zion, being taken up.

f.g: Changed and taken to heaven without tasting death.

chapters.n: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Anyone who comes to Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who sincerely seek Him.

f.w: without faith it is impossible to please him

chapters.n: By faith Noah, warned by God about things not yet seen, reverently built an ark to save his family. His faith condemned the unbelieving world, and he inherited the righteousness that comes by faith.
By faith Abraham obeyed when called to leave home for a land he would inherit, even though he didn’t know where he was going.
By faith he lived in the promised land like a foreigner, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, who shared the same promise.
He was looking forward to a city with permanent foundations, designed and built by God.
By faith even Sarah, past childbearing age, received power to conceive, because she trusted that God would keep His promise.
So from one man, as good as dead in age, came descendants as many as the stars and countless as sand on the seashore.

f.w: as the stars of the sky

f.g: Past the age of fathering children.

chapters.n: All these died still holding to faith, without having received the full promises. They saw them from a distance, welcomed them, and admitted they were strangers and pilgrims on earth.
People who speak this way show they are searching for a homeland.
If they had been thinking of the country they left, they could have gone back.
Instead they longed for a better country — a heavenly one. So God isn’t ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.

f.w: God is not ashamed to be called their God

chapters.n: By faith Abraham, when tested, offered up Isaac. The one who had received the promises was ready to sacrifice his only son.

f.g: Unique, one-of-a-kind son of promise — a type of the Father offering His Son.

chapters.n: This was the son of whom God had said, “Through Isaac your descendants will be named.”

f.w: That in Isaac shall thy seed be called

chapters.n: Abraham reasoned that God could even raise the dead, and in a sense he did receive Isaac back from death — a symbol of Christ’s Resurrection.

f.g: Figuratively, as a symbol or type.

f.w: God was able to raise him up

chapters.n: By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau about their futures.
By faith Jacob, as he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshipped, leaning on the top of his staff.

f.w: blessed both the sons of Joseph
leaning upon the top of his staff

chapters.n: By faith Joseph, near death, spoke of the Israelites’ future exodus and gave instructions about burying his bones in the promised land.
By faith Moses’s parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw he was a special child and were not afraid of Pharaoh’s order.
By faith Moses, when he grew up, refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.
He chose to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy sin’s fleeting pleasures.
He considered disgrace for the sake of the Messiah more valuable than Egypt’s treasures, because he looked ahead to his reward. Restoration scripture shows Moses knew of Christ.
By faith he left Egypt, unafraid of the king’s anger, persevering as though he saw the invisible God.

f.w: as seeing him who is invisible

chapters.n: By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the lamb’s blood, so the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s firstborn — a type of Christ’s protecting blood.
By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry ground; when the Egyptians tried to follow, they drowned.
By faith Jericho’s walls fell after Israel marched around them for seven days.

f.w: the walls of Jericho fell down

chapters.n: By faith Rahab, though a prostitute, was not destroyed with the disobedient, because she welcomed the Israelite spies in peace. Matthew lists her as an ancestor of Jesus.
The author runs out of time: he could tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets — imperfect people whose faith God still used.
Through faith they conquered kingdoms, did what was right, received promises, and shut lions’ mouths — as Daniel did.
They quenched raging fire, escaped the sword, gained strength out of weakness, became mighty in battle, and routed foreign armies.

f.w: out of weakness were made strong

chapters.n: Women received their dead back to life. Others were tortured and refused release, so they could gain a better resurrection.

f.w: Women received their dead raised to life again

chapters.n: Others faced cruel mocking and whipping, chains, and imprisonment.
They were stoned, sawn in two, killed by the sword. They wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, persecuted, mistreated. Jewish tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two.

f.g: Ancient Jewish tradition says this was Isaiah’s fate under King Manasseh.

chapters.n: The world wasn’t worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, living in caves and holes in the ground.

f.w: dens and caves of the earth

chapters.n: All these were commended for their faith, yet none received the full promise in their lifetime.

God planned something better, so that they would not be made perfect without us. Joseph Smith taught that the living and dead must be linked together for either to be made perfect — the doctrine behind temple work for the dead. The JST adds that they were perfected through their sufferings.

f.w: they without us should not be made perfect

f.g: JST: “some better things for them through their sufferings, for without sufferings they could not be made perfect.”

chapters.n: Since we are surrounded by such a huge crowd of faithful witnesses — the heroes of chapter 11, pictured like spectators in a stadium — let us throw off every burden and clinging sin and run our race with endurance.

f.g: A great crowd of those who testified by their faithful lives.

chapters.n: Keep your eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of our faith. For the joy ahead of Him, He endured the cross, scorning its shame, and now sits at the right hand of God’s throne.

f.g: Pioneer and completer — He began faith’s race and finished it perfectly.

f.w: for the joy that was set before him

chapters.n: Think about Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so you won’t grow weary and lose heart.
In your struggle against sin, you haven’t yet resisted to the point of shedding blood, as Jesus and the martyrs did.

f.g: Fought to the point of death.

chapters.n: Have you forgotten how scripture encourages you as children? “My son, don’t take the Lord’s discipline lightly or lose heart when He corrects you.”

f.w: despise not thou the chastening of the Lord

chapters.n: “For the Lord disciplines the one He loves and corrects every child He accepts.”

f.w: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth

chapters.n: Endure hardship as discipline. God is treating you as His children — what child isn’t corrected by a father?

f.w: God dealeth with you as with sons

chapters.n: If you never experienced discipline, which all children receive, you would be like illegitimate children without a caring father, not true sons and daughters.

f.g: Illegitimate children, who often lacked a father’s training and inheritance.

chapters.n: We respected our earthly fathers who disciplined us. How much more should we submit to the Father of our spirits and truly live? This verse supports the teaching that God is literally the Father of our spirits.
Our earthly fathers disciplined us briefly as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our true good, so we can share His holiness.
No discipline feels pleasant at the time — it hurts. But later it produces a peaceful harvest of righteousness for those trained by it.
So strengthen your drooping hands and weak knees.

f.w: lift up the hands which hang down

chapters.n: Make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame isn’t twisted out of joint but healed instead. Our choices help or hurt weaker members too.
Strive for peace with everyone, and for holiness — without which no one will see the Lord.

f.w: no man shall see the Lord

chapters.n: Watch out that no one falls short of God’s grace, and that no bitter root springs up to cause trouble and poison many.

f.w: fail of the grace of God
f.g: Fall short of, come up short.

chapters.n: Make sure no one is sexually immoral or irreverent like Esau, who traded his birthright for a single meal.

f.g: Godless, treating the sacred as common.

chapters.n: You know that later, when Esau wanted the blessing, he was rejected. He couldn’t undo what he had done, though he sought it with tears.

f.g: No way to change the outcome or reverse his father’s decision.

chapters.n: You haven’t come to a mountain that can be touched — Sinai — blazing with fire, gloom, darkness, and storm.

f.w: the mount that might be touched

chapters.n: Nor to a trumpet blast and a voice so overwhelming that the people begged not to hear another word.

f.w: entreated that the word should not be spoken to them any more

chapters.n: They couldn’t bear the command: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.”

f.w: if so much as a beast touch the mountain

chapters.n: The sight was so terrifying that even Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.”
Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to countless thousands of angels in joyful assembly.

You have come to the assembly of the Church of the Firstborn, whose names are written in heaven; to God, the Judge of all; and to the spirits of righteous people made perfect. D&C 76 echoes this language describing celestial heirs.

f.w: spirits of just men made perfect

chapters.n: And to Jesus, Mediator of the new covenant, and to His sprinkled blood, which speaks a better word than Abel’s. Abel’s blood cried for justice; Christ’s blood speaks mercy.

f.w: Jesus the mediator of the new covenant

chapters.n: Be sure you don’t reject the One who is speaking. If those who refused the warning on earth didn’t escape, we certainly won’t if we turn away from Him who warns from heaven.
His voice shook the earth at Sinai, but now He promises, “Once more I will shake not only the earth but heaven too.”

f.w: Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven

chapters.n: “Once more” means that created, shakable things will be removed, so that what cannot be shaken will remain.

f.w: those things which cannot be shaken

chapters.n: Since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful and serve God acceptably with reverence and awe.

f.w: a kingdom which cannot be moved

f.g: Let us be grateful (Greek charis also means thanks).

chapters.n: For our God is a consuming fire — holy and purifying.

f.w: our God is a consuming fire

chapters.n: The closing chapter turns practical. First: keep on loving one another as brothers and sisters.

f.g: Greek philadelphia — family affection among believers.

chapters.n: Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for some people have entertained angels without realizing it — as Abraham did.

f.g: Show hospitality — vital for traveling believers in an age of dangerous inns.

chapters.n: Remember prisoners as if you were in chains with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in a body that can suffer.

f.w: Remember them that are in bonds

chapters.n: Marriage should be honored by everyone and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.
Keep your life free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said, “I will never leave you or forsake you.”

f.w: I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee

chapters.n: So we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?”
Remember your leaders who taught you God’s word. Consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith.

f.w: them which have the rule over you

f.g: The outcome of their way of life — perhaps faithful deaths.

chapters.n: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Leaders change and die, but He never changes.

f.w: the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever

chapters.n: Don’t be swept away by various strange teachings. It is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by rules about food, which never helped those who kept them.

f.g: Foods — probably ritual meals or food laws.

chapters.n: We have an altar — Christ’s sacrifice — from which those who still serve in the old tabernacle system have no right to eat.

f.g: Likely Christ’s cross and sacrifice, received through the sacrament.

chapters.n: On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the animals whose blood the high priest carried into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp.
Likewise Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make the people holy by His own blood. Golgotha lay outside Jerusalem’s walls.
So let us go out to Him, outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore — willing to be outsiders for Christ.
For here we have no permanent city; we are looking for the city that is to come.
Through Jesus, let us continually offer God a sacrifice of praise — the fruit of lips that confess His name.

f.g: Words of praise as an offering.

chapters.n: Don’t forget to do good and share with others, for God is pleased with such sacrifices.

f.w: with such sacrifices God is well pleased

chapters.n: Follow your leaders and support them. They keep watch over your souls and will give an account, so let them do it with joy, not groaning — which wouldn’t help you.
Pray for us. We are sure we have a clear conscience and want to live honorably in every way.
The author especially asks for prayers that he may be returned to them soon — perhaps he was in prison or otherwise prevented.
May the God of peace — who brought our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the sheep, back from the dead through the blood of the eternal covenant —
— equip you with everything good to do His will, working in us what pleases Him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever.

f.g: Equip, mend, make complete — like mending nets.

chapters.n: The author asks them to bear with his word of encouragement, adding that he has written only briefly. “Word of exhortation” suggests Hebrews began as a sermon.
Timothy has been released from prison, and if he arrives soon the author will bring him along to visit.
Greet all your leaders and all the Saints. Believers from Italy send greetings — perhaps Italians away from home, or Christians in Italy.

f.g: Those from Italy — the phrase can mean either living in or originating from Italy.

chapters.n: The closing blessing: grace be with you all.
